title: Done or Not: Grading the Verifiers of Computer-Using Agents
author: Tatra Labs

sections.value:
Every pipeline that trains or evaluates a computer-using agent ends in the same question. The agent says it is done. Is it?
Something has to answer that thousands of times, and its answers become the reward in reinforcement learning, the filter in data curation and the number in the evaluation. Usually it is a vision-language model reading the agent's screenshots, or a script checking whatever state it can reach. Both judge from a partial view. A screenshot can show an edit that was never saved; a script can query a table that does not answer the question.

VeriCUA (Sun, Yu, Knop, Sinha, Kong, Kao, Kumar and Kamath, of Google and the University of Hong Kong, October 2026) proposes to treat verification as exploration. The verifier first inspects the context and writes a rubric of fine-grained requirements. Then, for each requirement still unresolved, it chooses a GUI check or a code check, and it combines what it finds under explicit evidence rules in which the agent's own report of success is a claim to verify, never evidence.
On AndroidWorld, verifying the live machine, it agrees with the reference labels 90.5% of the time against 78.4% for a VLM judge, and halves the false-positive rate, 7.7% against 15.4%. On ScienceBoard its false-positive rate of 5.4% is about a quarter of a generated checker's 21.7%. The paper links no code.

done-or-not is a test bed for that idea, exact enough to grade against and small enough to run in a couple of seconds. It simulates three computers whose hidden state the harness knows exactly: a desktop with files and an editor, a helpdesk web app whose database lives on a server, and a phone's settings and notification shade. Twelve task templates at ten seeds make 120 tasks, and scripted agents run each one under every failure mode that applies to it: 910 cases in eleven labelled modes, 240 of them genuinely done and 670 not.
A verifier sees the task, every screenshot and the agent's claim, and it may spend a budget of 12 on read-only probes. A fresh look through the GUI costs 3 and a code read costs 1, and what code can reach differs by computer: the whole disk on the desktop, settings over a debug bridge on the phone, and nothing at all on the web, where the database is someone else's server.

```text
done-or-not show w_close-02/optimistic_ui
  ...
  --- 3: set('status', 'Closed')
  [Helpdesk] Ticket #957 — Docking station not detected
    Status:    Closed
    ...
    ✓ Saved
  CLAIM     Done: I closed ticket #957.

done-or-not probe w_close-02/optimistic_ui gui open_ticket id=957
  [Helpdesk] Ticket #957 — Docking station not detected
    Status:    Pending
    ...
```

The page said Saved. The server dropped the write. Every screenshot the agent took looks exactly like a real success, and only a fresh page load shows that it is not one. Code cannot make that check either: asked to read the database, the probe answers that it lives on a remote server and the verifier's sandbox has no credentials for it.

## Each judge has a column that defeats it

| accuracy | server only | unsaved edit | reverted | optimistic UI |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| explorer | 1.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 |
| code only | **0.00** | 1.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 |
| all screenshots, strict | 1.00 | 1.00 | **0.00** | **0.00** |
| all screenshots, lenient | 1.00 | 0.75 | **0.00** | **0.00** |
| last screenshot, strict | **0.00** | 1.00 | 1.00 | **0.00** |
| last screenshot, lenient | 1.00 | **0.00** | **0.00** | **0.00** |

Read the table by column; each cell is the share of that mode's cases the verifier got right. Code alone cannot reach the helpdesk server, so it rejects every web success it cannot confirm, and it scores 1.00 on optimistic UI for the wrong reason: it rejects those because it cannot see them either. Judges that read every screenshot catch nearly everything an agent did on screen, side effects included, and are blind to whatever happened after the last frame, when a sync, an automation rule or battery saver undid the change.
Judges that read only the last screenshot trade one error for another. Strict ones fail real successes the last screen does not show. Lenient ones accept anything it does not contradict, so they pass every unsaved edit, because the editor's unsaved-change dot reads as absence of evidence rather than as a no.

The budget sweep says the paper's thesis more sharply than the table does: screenshots are history. A verifier that trusts them and probes only the requirements they left open never improves, however much budget it is given. One that re-checks what the screenshots seemed to settle reaches 1.000 at a budget of 3, which is one GUI probe or three code reads. Without the screenshots at all it gets there too, at twice the budget.

```bash
pip install -e .
done-or-not grade explorer      # 1.000 on all 910 cases
done-or-not table               # every built-in verifier
done-or-not grade --cmd "python examples/minimal_verifier.py"
done-or-not grade --llm my-model --base-url http://localhost:8000/v1
```

A verifier can be a Python class, any program that speaks JSON lines on stdin and stdout — [`examples/minimal_verifier.py`](https://github.com/tatra-labs/done-or-not/blob/main/examples/minimal_verifier.py) is a skeleton of about 30 lines that imports nothing from the package — or a model behind any OpenAI-compatible `/chat/completions` endpoint. The model sees the task, every screenshot, the claim, the probe catalogue and the budget, and answers each turn with one JSON object, a probe or a verdict. It never sees the case id, which names the failure mode.

What this is, plainly, is a harness and not evidence. The failure modes are designed, so the baselines' blind spots exist by construction: I built a world in which screenshots go stale, and screenshot judges fail when they do. The explorer's perfect score comes from the same hand that wrote the worlds and their view parsers. It shows that a perfect score is reachable, not that exploration is easy. What the harness does contribute is exact labels, from an oracle over the full hidden state; controls that pin the floor, with always-accept and always-reject scoring exactly the base rates, 0.264 and 0.736, at a balanced accuracy of 0.500; and one shared set of evidence rules, so the rows compare evidence sources rather than prompts.
It is not VeriCUA. The paper runs real desktop, mobile and web environments with real agent trajectories, and a model builds each rubric from context; here the task text follows a fixed grammar and the rubric is parsed, so rubric quality is not under test. The evidence rules are this repository's reading of the paper's. And no LLM verifier has been graded here yet. The adapter ships and is tested against a scripted local server, but running a real one costs money I did not spend, and that is where the interesting numbers will come from.
